questions.question: On a number line, the gap from 0 to −1 is split into 4 equal parts, and a dot is placed 3 parts to the left of 0. Which of these three names sit exactly at the dot: −3/4, (−3)/4, 3/(−4)?
options: all three of them
−3/4 and (−3)/4 only
just −3/4 alone
just 3/(−4) alone
questions.explain: A single negative sign on the top, on the bottom, or out in front all give the same value, −3/4, so all three names land on the same dot. The trap is thinking that moving the sign moves the point.

questions.question: A number line is marked from −10 to 10 in steps of 1. Point A is at −7 and point B is at −2. Which point is farther to the left, and what does that tell you?
options: A, since −7 > −2
A, since −7 < −2
B, since 2 < 7
B, since −2 < −7
questions.explain: Farther left always means smaller: −7 sits 7 steps below 0 while −2 sits only 2 steps below, so −7 < −2. The trap is ordering negatives by their size without looking at the sign.

questions.question: On a number line, the gap between 0 and −1 is split into 5 equal parts. A dot sits 2 parts to the left of 0. Which of these is NOT another name for the position of the dot?
questions.explain: Two parts left of 0 out of 5 is −2/5, which is also −0.4, (−2)/5 and 2/(−5). But −2/(−5) has two negatives, which cancel to make positive 2/5, on the right side of 0.

questions.question: On a number line, the gap between −1 and 0 is split into 10 equal parts. Point P is 3 parts to the left of 0 and point Q is 8 parts to the left of 0. Which statement is true?
options: Q is right of P, so −0.8 > −0.3
P is right of Q, but −0.8 > −0.3
Q is right of P, so −0.3 > −0.8
P is right of Q, so −0.3 > −0.8
questions.explain: P at −0.3 is only 3 parts from 0 while Q at −0.8 is 8 parts away, so P is to the right and −0.3 > −0.8. On the negative side, the number with the bigger digits is the smaller number.

questions.question: Which of these numbers is farthest to the left on a number line?
questions.explain: Write them all as decimals: −0.65, −0.6, −0.7, and −3/(−4) = +0.75. The most negative is −0.7. Watch for −3/(−4): two negatives make a positive, so it is on the right of 0.

questions.question: Which pair of rational numbers sits at the SAME point on a number line?
questions.explain: One negative sign, whether on the top, the bottom, or in front, gives the same value, so −5/8 and 5/(−8) are the same point. Two negatives cancel, so (−5)/(−8) is positive 5/8, on the other side of 0.

questions.question: Put these numbers in order from farthest left to farthest right on a number line: 0.6, −4/3, 3/(−4), −1.5. Which list is correct?
questions.explain: As decimals they are 0.6, −1.33, −0.75 and −1.5, so from left to right: −1.5, −4/3, 3/(−4), 0.6. Remember 3/(−4) is negative, and among negatives the bigger digits sit farther left.

questions.question: Which of these rational numbers lies to the LEFT of −1 on a number line?
questions.explain: 5/(−4) equals −1.25, which is farther below 0 than −1, so it sits to the left of −1. −4/5 and −0.95 are closer to 0 than −1 is, and −5/(−4) has two negatives, so it is positive 1.25.

questions.question: Ava records the overnight low in Kamloops for four nights: Monday −4.5 °C, Tuesday −9/2 °C, Wednesday −7/(−2) °C, Thursday −3.25 °C. She places all four on a number line. Which night was coldest, and which night was above freezing?
options: Monday and Tuesday tie; Wednesday above freezing
Thursday is coldest; Wednesday is above freezing
Monday and Tuesday tie; no night is above freezing
Tuesday is coldest; Wednesday is above freezing
questions.explain: −9/2 is −4.5, so Monday and Tuesday share the coldest point, and −7/(−2) has two negatives, so it is +3.5 °C, above freezing. The trap is thinking −3.25 is coldest because 3.25 has the smallest digits.

questions.question: Four students mark their school snack-account balances on one number line, in dollars: Noah −3/4, Sam 3/(−4), Ella −0.7, Ravi −0.8. Two of them land on the exact same point. Who is immediately to the RIGHT of that shared point?
options: Noah
Ella
Ravi
Sam
questions.explain: Noah and Sam are both at −0.75, since 3/(−4) equals −3/4. Ella at −0.7 is closer to 0, so she is just to the right of them; Ravi at −0.8 is farther left even though 0.8 looks bigger than 0.75.

questions.question: Kai says: on a number line, −7.5 must be to the right of −2.5 because 7.5 is bigger than 2.5. What is wrong with Kai's thinking?
options: Nothing, since 7.5 > 2.5 puts it farther right
It is only wrong because decimals are not integers
−7.5 is farther left, since it is 7.5 below zero
It is right of −2.5, but only by 5 units, not 7.5
questions.explain: For negatives, bigger digits after the sign mean farther below 0, so −7.5 sits farther left than −2.5 and is the smaller number. Comparing 7.5 and 2.5 without their signs gives the backwards answer.

questions.question: Mia marks −5/6 on a number line. Then she says 5/(−6) must go at a different point because the negative sign is in a different spot. Which statement is correct?
options: Different point; 5/(−6) belongs at −6/5, past the point −1
Different point; 5/(−6) is positive since only 6 is negative
Same point, but only because both are close to the point −1
Same point; one negative anywhere gives the value −5/6
questions.explain: A single negative sign, on the top, the bottom, or out in front, gives the same rational number, so −5/6 and 5/(−6) are one point. Only two negatives, like (−5)/(−6), would flip it to the positive side.
